implementation_notes: Python replaces the boundary attribute in place: patch.object(TimeDisplay, 'now', return_value=...) (or patch('pkg.mod.clock')) swaps it for the duration of the test and restores it automatically, and pytest's monkeypatch.setattr does the same without a context manager - the pytest docs recommend patching the name where the SUT looks it up and making dependencies explicit where you control the code. A test-only subclass (class TimeDisplayTss(TimeDisplay): def now(self): ...) is ordinary Python and remains useful when the fake must be constructed, passed where a real TimeDisplay is expected, or carry configuration shared by several tests.
code_sketch:
def test_midnight(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(TimeDisplay, "now", lambda self: FIXED)
    assert TimeDisplay().get_current_time_as_html_fragment() == MIDNIGHT

with patch.object(TimeDisplay, "now", return_value=FIXED):   # stdlib equivalent
    assert TimeDisplay().get_current_time_as_html_fragment() == MIDNIGHT
pitfalls: patch('module.name') must name the attribute where it is looked up (the SUT's module), not where it was defined - patch('mypkg.display.time', ...), not patch('time.time', ...).

A subclass override only affects calls dispatched through the instance (self.now()); a module-level call such as time.time() inside the method body is untouched by the subclass and must be patched instead.
Decorators pass extra mock arguments into the test signature while context managers do not; mixing both in one test is a common source of argument-shift confusion.
